subject: Chemistry
title: TNT: The Standard Explosive
description: A 60-second lesson on TNT: The Standard Explosive.

hook.text: TNT is so stable you can hit it with a hammer and it won't explode. It needs a detonator to go off.

buildup.text: Trinitrotoluene was first made in 1863 by a German chemist. For years, nobody realized it was explosive.

discovery.text: When detonated, TNT decomposes instantly into gases that expand at 6,900 meters per second.

twist.text: It was used as a yellow dye before anyone discovered its explosive power. Imagine dying fabric with TNT.

climax.text: All explosives are now measured in 'tons of TNT equivalent.' It became the universal yardstick of destruction.

punchline.text: First a dye, then a bomb, now a unit of measurement.

quiz.question: What was TNT originally used for before its explosive power was discovered?

details.summary: Trinitrotoluene, or TNT, became the standard military and industrial explosive due to its remarkable stability during storage and transport combined with powerful detonation energy. Its consistent blast yield made it the universal benchmark for measuring explosive force.
details.whyItMatters: TNT's predictability revolutionized both mining and military operations. The 'ton of TNT' remains the standard unit for comparing explosive yields, from demolition charges to nuclear weapons.
takeaways: TNT is valued for stability during handling and transport
It requires a detonator to explode, unlike more sensitive compounds
Explosive yields are still measured in TNT equivalents today

faq.question: Why is TNT used as the standard reference for explosive power?
faq.answer: TNT produces a consistent, well-measured energy release of approximately 4.184 megajoules per kilogram. Its predictable detonation velocity and widespread historical use made it the natural reference point for expressing explosive yields of all other materials.

faq.question: Is TNT still widely used today or has it been replaced?
faq.answer: TNT remains in use but is increasingly supplemented by compositions like C-4 and ammonium nitrate-fuel oil mixtures for specific applications. Its role as the universal measurement standard persists even as newer explosives outperform it.
